title: Expressions with get
subtitle: get down to, get over, get rid of, get your own back
summary: Use the many meanings of get, its phrasal verbs and its fixed expressions, and replace them with more formal words when you need to.

lesson.heading: The three basic meanings of get
lesson.text: **Get** is one of the most frequent verbs in spoken English. Its basic meanings are receive or obtain, change position, and change state.

examples.text: Please **get** me a sandwich when you're in town.
I **got** a text from John today.

lesson.heading: More specific meanings
lesson.text: In some fixed patterns **get** has a much narrower meaning. Each of these could be replaced by a more formal verb, which is what you do in writing.

examples.text: It's my turn to **get** dinner tonight.
I don't **get** it. Why did he speak like that?
His behaviour really **gets** me at times.
I saw Harry's new girlfriend but I didn't **get to** speak to her.
Once we **got to know** each other, we became great friends.
You **get** the phone and I'll **get** the door.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with get 1
rows: fail to do something by a certain time
begin to give serious attention to
be successful with an application, e.g. to a university

lesson.heading: Examples of those verbs
lesson.text: Note the difference between **get down** (depress) and **get down to** (start work on something seriously).

examples.text: It was difficult to **get** my point of view **across** to the committee.
I hope the inquiry will **get at** the truth.
It's time you **got down to** some work.
She did well in her exams and **got into** university.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with get 2
rows: finally do something you have long intended to do
come to a successful end; also use up all of
lesson.note: However will we get on without you? / Jo is getting on very well at school. / He got through his month's salary in one weekend.

lesson.heading: Other expressions with get
rows: **get out of bed on the wrong side**
be in a bad mood all day
**get off to a good / bad start**

lesson.text: Get is fine in speech, but in formal writing choose a precise verb instead: get me = annoy me, get over = recover from, get this book = buy this book.

exercises.prompt: Match the get expression with a more formal equivalent.

pairs.left: I'll never get to do it.
I got a text from John.

exercises.prompt: Although they had only told their parents, the news soon got ___ the village.
exercises.explanation: Get round = spread, of news or gossip.

exercises.prompt: She made a good impression, so she has got ___ to the second round of interviews.
exercises.explanation: Get through = come to a successful end, pass a stage.

exercises.prompt: I have an essay to write but I'm finding it hard to get ___ it.
exercises.explanation: Get down to something = begin to give it serious attention.

exercises.prompt: I've been meaning to redecorate my room for ages but I just can't get ___ it.
exercises.explanation: Get round to = finally do something you have intended to do for a long time.

exercises.prompt: What have you been getting ___ since we last met?
exercises.explanation: Get up to = do, often something bad or mischievous.

exercises.prompt: Surely you haven't got ___ all the biscuits already?
exercises.explanation: Get through also means use up all of something.

exercises.prompt: The new political party was finding it difficult to get its message ___ to the public.
exercises.explanation: Get an idea across = communicate it successfully.

exercises.prompt: I was ill last semester and I got seriously ___ with my studies.
exercises.explanation: Get behind with something = fail to do it by the time you should.

exercises.prompt: If this continues, I probably won't get ___ university this year.
exercises.explanation: Get into a university = be accepted there.

exercises.prompt: We're having a get-___ on Friday to celebrate Jan's birthday.
exercises.explanation: A get-together is an informal meeting or party.

exercises.statement: His progress on the guitar was slow at first, but he's getting on well now.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with the natural reply.

pairs.left: Someone has been very impolite to your friend.
Someone is about to throw something away.
pairs.right: Don't get rid of that yet!

pairs.left: Someone is negative about everything you suggest.
pairs.right: You got out of bed on the wrong side this morning!

pairs.left: Someone has done something very cruel to you.
pairs.right: You wait! I'll get my own back on you one day!

pairs.left: Someone won't help clear up after the party.
pairs.right: You always try to get out of things!

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. (The meeting started badly because of Elliot's speech.)
exercises.answer: The meeting got off to a bad start
exercises.explanation: Get off to a good or bad start = begin well or badly.
